title: Idiomatic Expressions and Phrases
tagline: Year 3 — Common English idioms: meaning, usage in a sentence and how to guess an unfamiliar one

introduction.overview: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is not the sum of its words. "Spill the beans" has nothing to do with beans. Idioms are common in questions because they test whether you know natural English. Some can be guessed from the picture they paint; many must be learned. This chapter organises common idioms by theme and shows how to use the sentence to confirm the meaning.
introduction.placementRelevance: Idiom questions appear in the verbal sections of bank, SSC and campus tests.
introduction.realWorldContext: Business English is full of idioms ("the ball is in your court", "cut corners"); understanding them avoids miscommunication.

learningObjectives: Use sentence context to confirm a meaning
Guess the meaning from the picture the idiom paints
Use idioms correctly in your own writing

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: An idiom is fixed: changing its words usually destroys the meaning.

coreDefinitions: Idiom: a phrase with a figurative meaning.
Literal meaning: the plain meaning of the words.
Figurative meaning: the intended, non-literal meaning.
Context: the sentence that supplies clues.
Fixed phrase: a group of words that cannot be varied.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Picture the idiom and ask what situation it describes. The picture usually points to the meaning.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Read the sentence, ignore the literal meaning, ask what situation the idiom stands for, and match that with the options.

mainNarrative: "The speaker told a joke to break the ice at the start of the meeting." Breaking the ice means starting a conversation in an awkward or formal situation.
"He will bite the bullet and tell his manager about the mistake." To bite the bullet is to do something unpleasant that cannot be avoided, with courage.
"She has been burning the midnight oil to finish her thesis." To burn the midnight oil is to work late at night.
"The elephant in the room" is an obvious, important problem that everyone avoids discussing.
If you do not know an idiom, use the sentence: "Stop beating around the bush and tell me what happened" calls for a direct answer, so beating around the bush means avoiding the main point.

deepDiveAspects.title: Idioms by theme
deepDiveAspects.content: Grouping idioms by theme (secrets, effort, cost, decision) makes them easier to recall.

deepDiveAspects.title: Avoid literal traps
deepDiveAspects.content: Wrong options often give the literal meaning of the words.

easy.question:
The speaker told a joke to break the ice at the start of the meeting.

The idiom "break the ice" in this sentence means
options: ease the tension and begin the conversation
easy.correctAnswer: ease the tension and begin the conversation
easy.explanation: A joke at the start eases the awkwardness so that people can talk.

easy.question:
Passing the quiz was a piece of cake for her.

The idiom "a piece of cake" in this sentence means
easy.explanation: The idiom means something that is extremely easy to do.

easy.question:
We go to that restaurant once in a blue moon.

The idiom "once in a blue moon" in this sentence means
easy.explanation: It means very rarely, not literally on the occasion of a blue moon.

intermediate.question:
She has been burning the midnight oil to finish her thesis.

The idiom "burning the midnight oil" in this sentence means
intermediate.explanation: It means working late at night.

intermediate.question:
He decided to bite the bullet and tell his manager about the mistake.

The idiom "bite the bullet" in this sentence means
intermediate.explanation: It means to do something difficult or unpleasant that cannot be avoided.

intermediate.question:
The designer jewellery cost an arm and a leg.

The idiom "cost an arm and a leg" in this sentence means
intermediate.explanation: It means to cost a very large amount.

advanced.question:
After three failed attempts, he threw in the towel.

The idiom "threw in the towel" in this sentence means
advanced.explanation: To throw in the towel is to give up.

advanced.question:
Nobody mentioned the budget crisis, though it was the elephant in the room.

The idiom "the elephant in the room" in this sentence means
options: an obvious problem that no one wants to discuss
advanced.correctAnswer: an obvious problem that no one wants to discuss
advanced.explanation: It refers to a major issue that everyone knows about but avoids.

placementStyle.question:
Losing that job turned out to be a blessing in disguise.

The idiom "a blessing in disguise" in this sentence means
options: something that seems bad but turns out good
placementStyle.correctAnswer: something that seems bad but turns out good
placementStyle.explanation: It describes a misfortune that brings an unexpected benefit.

placementStyle.question:
By quarrelling with every client, he burned his bridges in the industry.

The idiom "burned his bridges" in this sentence means
options: destroyed the chance of returning or getting help
placementStyle.correctAnswer: destroyed the chance of returning or getting help
placementStyle.explanation: It means ruining relationships so that return is impossible.

placementStyle.question:
I don't believe it, but let me play devil's advocate and argue the other side.

The idiom "play devil's advocate" in this sentence means
options: argue the opposite view for the sake of argument
placementStyle.correctAnswer: argue the opposite view for the sake of argument
placementStyle.explanation: It means arguing against a view, often to test it, without necessarily believing the argument.
